title: Sundial Conflux profiling notebook
content:
Purpose:
Quick personal log of small-scale experiments aimed at understanding interaction between arrival phase alignment (conflux/wave alignment) and continuous batching on p95/p99 latency for 13B decoder-only models running on A100-80GB. Trying to capture reproducible steps, observations, and immediate next actions.

High-level hypothesis:
- When request arrivals have a persistent low-frequency phase alignment (i.e., bursts that repeatedly line up with batching window boundaries), continuous-batching can either amplify tail latency (if many requests queue up) or improve average latency (if batching reduces kernel overhead).
- Adding a small randomized jitter to batch cut (0-3ms) and using adaptive batch timeout (based on recent interarrival) will reduce p99 without hurting p50.

Test harness details:
- Model: llama-ish-13b-float16 (baseline) and quantized-int8 variant (q8_0).
- Hardware: single A100-80GB (shared local testbed), CUDA 11.8, Triton-like runtime (local dev build), runtime branch: "sundial-profiles".
- Runner: synthetic client in Go (github link above), supports composition of arrival waveforms: sinusoid, clustered Poisson, manual multi-pulse.
- Measurement windows: 10 runs x 180s each; discard first 30s as warmup.
- Metrics captured: qps, p50, p95, p99, GPU util, avg batch size, batch timeout triggered fraction, queuing time distribution.

Experiment matrix (primary grid):
- Arrival patterns: (A) steady Poisson @ 60 qps, (B) low-frequency sinusoid 40-120 qps (period 60s), (C) 3-pulse conflux (3 spikes every 45s, each spike 400ms long at 200 qps).
- Batch timeout (ms): 2, 6, 12 (2ms is aggressive, 12ms conservative).
- Batch size cap: 8, 16, 32
- Model variant: float16, q8_0

Representative run (conflux spikes, float16, timeout=6ms, cap=16):
- Nominal qps (windowed): mean 65 qps; spikes up to 180 qps during 400ms pulses.
- Avg batch size: 12 during spikes, 6 during baseline windows.
- GPU util (avg over run): 78% (peaks 96% during pulses).
- p50: 22ms, p95: 84ms, p99: 210ms.
- Queuing time median: 9ms; queuing tail (99.9th): 320ms (rare multi-batch coalescence events).
- Observed behavior: when conflux pulses align with internal batch cut boundary (every N ms depending on timeout), we see a 2-3x jump in p99 for a 1-2 second window after each pulse.

Contrast: same config but timeout=2ms:
- Avg batch size drops to 8 during spikes; GPU util avg 64%.
- p50: 18ms, p95: 62ms, p99: 140ms.
- Conclusion: lower timeout reduces tail but reduces GPU efficiency.

Quantized model (q8_0) with timeout=6ms:
- Throughput capacity increases ~15% at same GPU util; avg batch size ~same.
- p50 ~20ms, p95 ~78ms, p99 ~195ms (slightly better tail than float16, likely due to faster kernel execution reducing queuing build-up).

Experiment: add randomized batch-cut jitter (uniform 0-3ms) + adaptive timeout (timeout = median interarrival * 0.7 clamped [2,12ms])
- Result on conflux pattern: p99 reduced from 210ms -> 95ms (float16), p95 from 84ms -> 58ms.
- Avg batch size: 9 -> 10 (slight drop), GPU util steady 72% (good tradeoff).
- Interpretation: jitter breaks pathological alignment; adaptive timeout auto-tunes to baseline rate and avoids overbuffering during spikes.

Edge-case: batch cap=32 + timeout=12ms (worst compaction)
- p99 runaway: 420-600ms during sustained spike clusters; large batches (20-30) create long kernel times which amplify queuing for subsequent arrivals.

Quick table (selected runs):
- run1: conflux, timeout2, cap16, float16 -> p50 18ms, p95 62ms, p99 140ms, qps mean 70
- run2: conflux, timeout6, cap16, float16 -> p50 22ms, p95 84ms, p99 210ms, qps mean 65
- run3: conflux, timeout6+jitter+adaptive, cap16, float16 -> p50 19ms, p95 58ms, p99 95ms, qps mean 68
- run4: sinusoid, timeout6, cap32, q8_0 -> p50 24ms, p95 70ms, p99 165ms, qps mean 85
- run5: poisson, timeout2, cap8, q8_0 -> p50 14ms, p95 40ms, p99 88ms, qps mean 60

Observations and rules of thumb from the lab:
1) Batch timeout is the primary lever for tail vs GPU-efficiency tradeoff. 2-4ms aggressively minimizes tail in most low-latency workloads; 8-12ms is better for throughput-first (but watch p99).
2) Deterministic arrival alignment (periodic spikes) is a real failure mode for continuous-batching: small jittering of batch cuts yields large reductions in p99.
3) Quantized kernels help tail modestly by shortening per-batch kernel time; they are not a panacea — queuing policy still matters.
4) Large batch caps (>=32) can catastrophically amplify p99 under clustered arrivals because kernel durations become long and block subsequent batches.

Immediate next experiments to run (priority order):
- A: Run conflux runs with jitter+adaptive on 2xA100 (multi-GPU) to see cross-GPU queuing effects (does jitter still help when requests can be routed to an idle GPU?).
- B: Try Poisson+periodic background maintenance spikes (simulate control-plane / healthcheck noise) to test robustness.
- C: Explore exponential backoff for batch building: if queued time exceeds threshold, force dispatch smaller batch to protect tail.
- D: Profile GPU kernel time distribution (detailed per-batch timeline) for q8_0 vs float16 to quantify kernel skew as a source of tail.

Notes-to-self / reproducibility checklist:
- Save runner args and seed for waveform generator under experiments/sundial/ (not checked in yet).
- Attach telemetry trace id for runs with extreme p99.
- Add a small harness change: capture per-batch creation timestamp + dispatch timestamp + kernel-complete timestamp to correlate batch size -> kernel duration -> subsequent queue growth.

Action items:
- File a short RFC for adopting batch-cut jitter as a default in the runtime for med/high-concurrency single-GPU modes (dry perf numbers attached above). Owner: Drew.
- Share 1-pager with perf channel and SRE: initial advocate: Maya.
- Implement small adaptive-timeout prototype in branch "sundial-adaptive" and run multi-GPU experiments.

Random TODOs (housekeeping):
- Clean up log naming to include arrival-pattern label + seed + timeout param.
- Run a longer 1-hour stability run for the promising jitter+adaptive config and inspect memory/GPU temp drift.

Closing note:
This scratch captures the initial evidence that small randomness in batching and mild adaptivity are high-leverage changes to reduce tail under real-world-ish periodic surges. Still lots to validate across hardware and model sizes.

---
End of notebook entry (scratch).
summary: Personal scratchpad: experiments on arrival alignment (conflux) vs continuous batching; found jitter+adaptive timeout reduces p99 significantly with modest GPU util tradeoffs. Next: multi-GPU and kernel profiling.
